about: Authored flashcard deck (memory plan 2026-09-29). Each family has a front, back, memory anchor, shape and items with a named misconception.

families.front: What does 3G do? What does G on its own do?
families.back: 3G jumps to line 3, counted from the top of the file, wherever the cursor is now. G on its own jumps to the last line of the file.
families.anchor: G = ground floor: the bottom of the file. A number in front picks the floor, counted from the top.
families.shape: {N}G = line N from the top · G alone = the last line

items.prompt: The cursor is on line 5. You type 3G. Where does the cursor go?
choices: to line 8, three lines further down
to the end of the third block of art
why: 3G always means line 3, counted from the top. Where you start does not matter.
Moving three lines down from here is 3j. G counts from the top of the file.
G counts lines, not blocks. On its own G is the last line of the whole file.
Three lines up from here is 3k. 3G is line 3 from the top.
items.misconception: 3G read as a move relative to the cursor, or as 'three blocks'

items.prompt: The cursor is on line 1. Turn the first glyph of line 3 into #.

trap_answers.why: 3j moves three lines down from line 1, so it lands on line 4. 3G goes to line 3.

items.misconception: {N}j (N lines down from here) used where {N}G (line N) was meant

families.front: Where does gg go? And where does G go?
families.back: gg goes to the first line of the file. G goes to the last line. With a number both mean that line: 4gg and 4G both go to line 4.
families.anchor: gg = the top floor; G = ground floor at the bottom.
families.shape: gg = the first line · G = the last line

items.prompt: The cursor is on line 2 of this 5-line art. Where do gg and G each take it?
choices: gg to line 1, G to line 5
gg to line 5, G to line 1
gg to line 1, G one line down to line 3
gg to the start of line 2, G to the end of line 2
why: gg is the top of the file and G is the bottom.
That swaps them. G is the ground floor, at the bottom.
G without a number never means 'one line down'; that is j.
Both jump between lines. The start and end of this row are 0 and $.
items.misconception: top and bottom swapped, or G read as a move along the row

families.front: 3j or 3G?
families.back: 3j moves three lines down from where the cursor is. 3G jumps to line 3 no matter where the cursor is.
families.anchor: j hangs down below the line, like its hook: j = down.
families.shape: {N}j = N lines down from here · {N}G = line N from the top

items.prompt: The cursor is on line 2. You type 3j, and then 3G. Which line is it on after each?
why: 3j counts from the cursor (2 + 3 = 5). 3G counts from the top.
3G does not add to where you are; it is line 3 from the top.
3j is not a line number; it moves three lines down from line 2.
The number in front of G is the line. Only G alone means the last line.
items.misconception: the number in front of G and j read the same way

families.front: What does fo do?
families.back: fo moves right along the CURRENT row to the next o. If this row has no o, nothing happens: the cursor stays. ; repeats the find on the same row.
families.anchor: f = run your finger along this row.
families.shape: f{char} = this row only · /text<CR> = the whole file

items.prompt: The cursor is at the start of line 1, which has no o. The only o is on line 2. You type fo. What happens?
choices: nothing: the cursor stays on line 1
the cursor jumps to the o on line 2
the cursor jumps to the end of line 1
an o is typed at the cursor
why: f only looks along the row the cursor is on. No o on this row, so no move.
Searching the whole file is /o then Enter. f never leaves the row.
A failed f does not move at all. The end of the row is $.
f only moves; it never types. Typing needs i, a or o first.
items.misconception: f read as a whole-file search

items.prompt: The cursor is on line 1. Change the o on line 3 into O. Line 1 has no o.

trap_answers.why: fo only searches line 1, which has no o, so the cursor stays and rO changes the | under it. Go to the row first (3G), or search the file with /o<CR>.

items.misconception: f expected to find a glyph on another row

families.front: What does /o then Enter do?
families.back: / opens a search line at the bottom of the screen. Type the text; Enter jumps to the next match anywhere in the file, even rows below. n jumps to the match after that.
families.anchor: / = search the whole file.
families.shape: /text<CR> = the next match in the file · n = the one after

items.prompt: The next o is two rows below the cursor. Which keys reach it?
why: / searches the whole file, so it can reach another row.
fo only looks along the current row.
o opens a new empty line below and starts typing.
ro replaces the cell under the cursor with o.
items.misconception: f and / treated as the same kind of search

families.front: What are the three jobs of $?
families.back: On its own, $ jumps to the end of the row (2G$ = the end of line 2). In a line range, $ is the last line (:1,3t$). At the end of a pattern, $ means 'only at the row end' (\s\+$ = spaces at the end).
families.anchor: $ = the end: the row end, the last line, or a wall the pattern must touch.
families.shape: $ = the end of the row · :1,3t$ = the last line · -$ in a pattern = only at the row end

items.prompt: The cursor is on line 4. You type 2G$. Where does it end up?
choices: on f, the last glyph of line 2
on n, two lines down at the end of the row
on the last line of the file
on c, the start of line 2
why: 2G is line 2 from the top; $ then goes to the end of that row.
2G is not 'two lines down'. Two down would be 2j.
$ on its own is the end of the ROW. The last line is G.
The start of the row would be 0 or ^. $ is the end.
items.misconception: 2G read as 'down two', or $ read as the last line

items.prompt: You run :%s/-$// on these rows. Which rows change?
choices: rows 1 and 3 lose their last -, row 2 is unchanged
every - on every row is deleted
only the first - on each row is deleted
on every row, the text from the first - to the end is deleted
why: $ is a wall: the - must touch the row end. Row 2 ends in d, so it stays.
Only a - right before the row end can match; the others stay.
The first - of a row is not at the end, so it cannot match.
$ is not 'up to the end'. The pattern is one - that touches the end.
items.misconception: pattern $ read as 'up to the end of the line'

items.prompt: The cursor is on line 1. Delete the last glyph of line 2.

trap_answers.why: 2j moves two lines down from line 1, to line 3. 2G is line 2.

items.misconception: {N}G and {N}j confused before $

families.front: What does 3yy copy? Does anything change on screen?
families.back: 3yy copies (yanks) three whole lines, starting with the cursor line. Nothing changes on screen until you put the copy somewhere with p or P.
families.anchor: yy = yank the line: the doubled letter means the whole line.
families.shape: [count] verb target: 3yy = yank 3 lines · then p puts them

items.prompt: The cursor is on line 1 of an 8-line file. What does 3yyGp do?
choices: copies lines 1-3, jumps to the last line, puts the copy below it
copies three lines and stops there
copies lines 1-3 and puts them below line 3
copies lines 1-3 and puts them at the top of the file
why: Three parts: 3yy copies, G goes to the last line, p puts below it.
That reads only 3yy. G then moves and p puts the copy.
G moved the cursor to the last line first, so p puts below line 8.
G is the bottom of the file, and p puts BELOW the cursor line.
items.misconception: 3yyGp read as only 'yank three lines'

items.prompt: The cursor is on line 1. Copy the first two lines to below the last line.

trap_answers.why: Without G the copy is put below line 1, not at the end.
P puts the copy ABOVE the cursor line, so it lands before the last line.

items.misconception: the move (G) or the direction of put (p/P) left out

families.front: After yy, where does p put the line? And P?
families.back: After copying whole lines, p puts them BELOW the cursor line and P puts them ABOVE it.
families.anchor: p = put below · P = Put above (the capital stands taller).
families.shape: p = below or after · P = above or before

items.prompt: You copied the line ab with yy. The cursor is on line 2. You type P. Where does ab appear?
choices: between 11 and 22, above the cursor line
between 22 and 33, below the cursor line
why: Capital P puts above the cursor line.
Below is lower-case p.
P uses the cursor line, not the end of the file. Go there first with G.
P adds a line; nothing is replaced.
items.misconception: p and P swapped

families.front: :s/o/O/g with nothing between : and s. Which lines change?
families.back: With nothing before s, :s changes the CURRENT line only. Put a range before s to reach more lines.
families.anchor: :s is a fill-in form: :{where}s/{find}/{replace}/{flags}.
families.shape: :{where}s/{find}/{replace}/{flags} · empty {where} = this line

items.prompt: The cursor is on line 2. You run :s/-/=/ once. What changes?
choices: only line 1, the first match in the file
why: No range before s means the current line only.
Every line needs a range: :%s/-/=/.
:s does not search the file for its first match; it works on the lines you give it.
The range is optional; without it you get the current line.
items.misconception: no range read as 'every line'

items.prompt: Change exactly the first three - into =. Leave the fourth - alone.

trap_answers.why: A number after :s counts LINES (three lines from here), not matches, so all four change.
g changes every match on the line: all four.

items.misconception: a number after :s read as a number of matches

families.front: How do you change every line? Only lines 4 to 6?
families.back: Put the lines BEFORE s. :%s/-/=/ = every line, because % means all of them. :4,6s/-/=/ = lines 4 to 6. No range = the current line.
families.anchor: % = 100% of the lines.
families.shape: :%s = every line · :4,6s = lines 4-6 · :s = this line

items.prompt: Replace every - with = on every row, with one : command.

trap_answers.why: Without g only the first - on each row changes.
No range: only the current line changes. % goes before s.

items.misconception: % placed after s, or g left out

items.prompt: Which command changes o to O on lines 4, 5 and 6 only?
why: The lines go between : and s.
Anything after the last divider is a flag or a line count, not the lines to change.
% is every line of the file.
Right after s comes the divider; the range must come before s.
items.misconception: the range written after s

families.front: What does the g at the end of :s/o/O/g change?
families.back: Without g, :s changes only the FIRST match on each line. With g it changes every match on each line. g never adds lines; the range picks the lines.
families.anchor: g flag = global on the line: every match on it.
families.shape: :s/{find}/{replace}/ = the first match per line · add g = every match

items.prompt: The cursor is on the row o-o-o. You run :s/o/O/ (no g). What is the row now?
why: Without g only the first match on the line changes.
Changing all three needs the g flag.
:s starts from the left of the row; the first match is the first o.
There is a match, so the first one changes.
items.misconception: g expected by default

families.front: What does the e in :%s/\s\+$//e do?
families.back: e keeps :s quiet when nothing matches. Without it, a search that finds nothing shows an error message. The edit itself is the same.
families.anchor: e flag = excuse the errors.
families.shape: :s/{find}/{replace}/e = no error message when nothing matches

items.prompt: No row ends in a space. What does the e change in :%s/\s\+$//e?
choices: no error message is shown; nothing is edited
it deletes to the end of every row
it edits every row even without a match
why: e only silences the 'pattern not found' error.
The pattern decides what is deleted, not e.
Rows without a match are never edited.
Asking first is the c flag.
items.misconception: e read as an edit instead of a quiet switch

families.front: In :%s/\s\+$//e, what is the job of / and of \?
families.back: / divides the parts of :s: s/find/replace/flags. \ inside the find part makes the NEXT letter special: \s = a space or tab, \+ = one or more of it. You type both keys yourself.
families.anchor: \ = a power-up for the next letter.
families.shape: s/{find}/{replace}/ · \s = space or tab · \+ = one or more

items.prompt: In :%s/\s\+$//e, what does \s mean?
choices: a space or tab: the \ makes the s special
why: \ powers up the next letter; \s matches a space or a tab.
The dividers are the / signs.
Without the \ it would be the letter s.
\ is a key you type. Escape is written <Esc>.
items.misconception: \ read as a divider or as Escape

items.prompt: In :s/o/O/g, which character separates the find part from the replace part?
why: / is the divider: s/find/replace/flags.
\ powers up the letter after it inside a pattern; it divides nothing.
$ is an end: the row end or the last line.
% before s means every line.
items.misconception: / and \ swapped

families.front: What do u and Ctrl-r do?
families.back: u undoes the last change: one step back. Ctrl-r (hold Ctrl, press r) redoes what u undid.
families.anchor: u = one step back. Ctrl-r = redo.
families.shape: u = undo one change · <C-r> = redo it

items.prompt: The row says cat. You type rX (Xat), then u (cat), then rZ (Zat). Which keys bring back Xat?
choices: none: Xat is gone for good
why: g- steps back in time across undo branches: Zat, then Xat.
u walks back along the newest branch only: Zat becomes cat.
Ctrl-r redoes an undo on this branch; after rZ there is nothing to redo.
Vim keeps both branches; g- and g+ reach them.
items.misconception: u expected to reach an older branch

items.prompt: The row was cat. Someone typed rX, u, rZ, so it says Zat. Bring back Xat.

trap_answers.why: u goes back along the newest branch, to cat. The Xat change is on the other branch: use g-.

items.misconception: the undo branch (g-) unknown

families.front: You undid a change, then made a new one. How do you get the undone version back?
families.back: u only walks back along the newest branch. The old change is on another branch. g- steps back in time across branches, g+ steps forward. :earlier 1 is the same as g-.
families.anchor: g- = a time machine across branches.
families.shape: u = back on this branch · g- / g+ = back / forward in time

items.prompt: After g- you are looking at an older version. Which key returns to the newest one?
why: g+ steps forward in time, back to the newer version.
u undoes a change; it moves further back, not forward.
gg moves the cursor to the first line; it does not touch history.
g- again goes even further back in time.
items.misconception: g+ and u confused

families.front: x or r=: which keeps the row the same width?
families.back: x deletes the cell under the cursor: the rest of the row shifts left. r{char} replaces it in place: the row keeps its width. In art, r keeps the columns lined up.
families.anchor: x = cross it out. r = replace in place.
families.shape: x = delete one cell (row shrinks) · r{char} = replace one cell

items.prompt: The row is |ab| and the cursor is on a. You type x. What is the row now?
why: x deletes the a and the rest of the row moves left.
Keeping a blank cell there is r then a space.
x is a command here, not a letter to type. Turning a into x is rx.
x deletes the cell under the cursor, not the end of the row.
items.misconception: x expected to keep the row width

items.prompt: The cursor is on the first cell. Turn the a into = without changing the row's width.

trap_answers.why: x deletes the a, so the row becomes || and loses a cell. r= replaces in place.

items.misconception: delete used where replace was meant

families.front: R==<Esc> or r=?
families.back: R types over the cells one by one until <Esc>; the row keeps its width. r{char} changes exactly one cell and returns to Normal mode by itself.
families.anchor: R = Replace until you stop.
families.shape: r{char} = one cell · R{text}<Esc> = many cells

items.prompt: The row is a--b and the cursor is on the first -. You type R==<Esc>. What is the row?
why: R overwrites two cells; the width stays the same.
Pushing text right is Insert mode (i).
That is r=: one cell only.
R only overwrites as many cells as you type.
items.misconception: R read as insert

families.front: What does o do?
families.back: o opens a NEW empty line below the cursor line and starts typing there; <Esc> ends. O opens the new line above.
families.anchor: o = open a line below.
families.shape: o{text}<Esc> = a new line below · O = above

items.prompt: The cursor is on line 1 of the rows ab and cd. You type o-<Esc>. What are the rows?
why: o opens a line right below the cursor line.
Typing at the start of the row is I.
o opens below the CURSOR line. The end of the file would be Go.
Typing at the end of the row is A.
items.misconception: o read as 'add at the end of the file'

families.front: What does :1,3t$ do?
families.back: It copies lines 1 to 3 and puts the copy below the last line. t means 'to'; here $ is the last line. :1,3t0 would put the copy at the top.
families.anchor: :t = copy lines To a place.
families.shape: :{from},{to}t{dest} = copy those lines below line {dest}

items.prompt: Copy lines 1 and 2 to below the last line with one : command.

trap_answers.why: 0 puts the copy above line 1. $ is the last line.

items.misconception: $ as a line (the last line) unknown

families.front: Does :set list change the file?
families.back: No. :set list only SHOWS hidden characters, such as spaces at the end of a row, as marks. The text is unchanged. Deleting them is still an edit: :%s/\s\+$//e or $x.
families.anchor: list = let me see the invisible.
families.shape: :set list / :set nolist = show / hide the marks · display only

items.prompt: A row ends with two spaces. You run :set list. What changed in the file?
choices: nothing: the spaces are only shown as marks
the row was cut at its last glyph
why: :set list changes the display, never the text.
Deleting them needs an edit such as :%s/\s\+$//e.
No option here turns spaces into tabs.
Nothing is cut; the marks only make the spaces visible.
items.misconception: :set list expected to clean the row

items.prompt: What does :set colorcolumn=8 do?
choices: paints screen column 8 as a ruler
lights the column the cursor is in
why: It is a painted ruler; the text is untouched.
Options like this one only change the display.
Jumping to column 8 is 8|.
That is cursorcolumn, which follows the cursor.
items.misconception: colorcolumn and cursorcolumn confused

families.front: 0 or ^: which one lands on the first glyph?
families.back: 0 jumps to column 1 of the row, even when it is a space. ^ jumps to the first glyph that is not a space.
families.anchor: 0 = column zero, the very edge. ^ = the first peak of ink.
families.shape: 0 = column 1 · ^ = the first glyph · $ = the end

items.prompt: The row is two spaces, then /\. The cursor is on the \. Where do 0 and ^ each go?
choices: 0 to the first space, ^ to the /
0 to the /, ^ to the first space
0 to the /, ^ to the end of the row
why: 0 is column 1 even when it is blank; ^ skips the spaces.
That swaps them: 0 never skips spaces.
Only ^ skips the leading spaces.
The end of the row is $.
items.misconception: 0 read as the first glyph

families.front: In 12|i|<Esc>, which | moves and which | is typed?
families.back: The first | comes after a number in Normal mode: 12| jumps to column 12. After i you are typing, so the second | is a bar glyph. With :set virtualedit=all the cursor can stand in empty columns past the row end.
families.anchor: {N}| = a fence post at column N.
families.shape: {N}| = column N · i{text}<Esc> = type before the cursor

items.prompt: In 12|i|<Esc>, what are the two | keys?
choices: the first jumps to column 12; the second is a typed bar
both are jumps to a column
the first is a typed bar; the second jumps
why: In Normal mode 12| is a move; after i every key types text.
Before i you are in Normal mode, so 12| moves the cursor.
After i, keys type text until <Esc>.
The order decides the job: move first, then type.
items.misconception: | read by its shape instead of by where it stands

items.prompt: A row has 3 cells. With virtualedit off, you type 9|. Where is the cursor?
choices: on a, because the move failed
why: Without virtualedit the cursor stops at the last real cell.
Standing in empty columns needs :set virtualedit=all first.
The move still goes as far right as the row allows.
| never changes rows.
items.misconception: empty columns expected to be reachable without virtualedit

families.front: What changes when you type "ap instead of p?
families.back: "ap tells Vim to paste the contents of register a. p still puts that text after the cursor (or below a whole line).
families.anchor: The quote picks the pocket; p places what is in it.
families.shape: "{reg}p = paste register {reg} · p = put after

items.prompt: You copied a small frame into register a, then place the cursor on line 2. What does "ap do?
choices: puts register a's frame after line 2
why: The quote and a select the named register; p then puts its contents after the cursor line.
Plain p uses the unnamed register, but "a changes the source first.
Macro recording starts with q, not a quote followed by p.
Letters after a quote name a register; they are not line numbers.
items.misconception: the register prefix was treated as decoration

families.front: How does "ay$ differ from y$?
families.back: Both yank from the cursor through the end of the row, but "ay$ stores the copy in register a so another register can be left untouched.
families.anchor: Read the prefix first: quote plus a chooses the pocket; the motion says what to copy.
families.shape: "{reg}y{motion} = copy using register {reg}

items.prompt: Read "ay$. What is selected and where is it stored?
choices: the rest of this row, in register a
the whole row, in the unnamed register
the next row, in register y
the text before the cursor, in register a
why: y is the copy operator, $ supplies the row-end motion, and "a selects register a.
A doubled yy copies a whole line; this command ends with a single motion instead.
The y is the operator, not a register name in this position.
$ travels toward the row end, so the selection runs rightward from the cursor.
items.misconception: the quote register and the motion were read as one command

families.front: What does % do when it stands before s in :%s?
families.back: % is the range for every line of the file. It is not the matching-bracket motion in that command-line position.
families.anchor: Percent means the whole file when it opens a colon command.
families.shape: %s = every line · % on its own = matching bracket

items.prompt: In :%s/-/=/g, which lines are searched?
choices: the line containing a matching bracket
why: Placed before s, % expands the range to all lines.
No range before s would mean only the current line.
Matching brackets are the Normal-mode job of a lone %.
The last line is written with $ as a line destination.
items.misconception: % was remembered only as the bracket-jump key

families.front: After f- and ;, what does , do?
families.back: , repeats the last f or t search in the reverse direction. It keeps the same target character but walks back along the row.
families.anchor: Semicolon follows the trail; comma walks the trail backward.
families.shape: ; = repeat forward · , = repeat backward

items.prompt: The row is a-b-c-d. From a, f- lands on the first dash and ; lands on the second. Where does , go?
choices: to the start of the row
why: Comma reverses the most recent f/t direction and returns to the previous dash.
The forward repeat is ;, so the third dash needs another semicolon.
Column 1 is 0, not comma.
Find repeats stay on the current row unless you explicitly move elsewhere.
items.misconception: the two repeat keys were treated as synonyms

families.front: What does a lone dot repeat?
families.back: . repeats the most recent change at the new cursor position. Motions used to reach that position do not become the repeated edit.
families.anchor: Dot is a stamp: make one change, move, stamp it again.
families.shape: . = repeat the last change

items.prompt: On two rows, rO changes the first cell of row 1. You press j. What does . do?
choices: changes the first cell of row 2 to O
types a literal dot in row 2
why: The edit rO is the last change; j only repositions the cursor before the stamp is used.
A motion does not undo the edit, and dot does not travel backward.
A dot types text only in Insert mode; in Normal mode it repeats a change.
Dot replays the change, not the navigation that preceded it.
items.misconception: dot was read as a literal glyph or as a motion replay

families.front: What does :4,6m0 do?
families.back: It removes lines 4 through 6 from their old place and moves them before line 1. The destination is 0, not a count of lines.
families.anchor: m relocates; the range is the luggage and the destination is the new shelf.
families.shape: :[from],[to]m{dest} = move those lines to {dest}

items.prompt: A six-line file receives :4,6m0. Where are those three lines afterward?
choices: at the top, before the old line 1
copied after line 6 while the originals stay
why: The range names lines 4-6 and destination 0 means before the first line.
Copying uses t; m removes the selected lines from their original position.
A destination of . means below the current line, while 0 means the top.
Moving preserves the lines; deletion would use d or :d.
items.misconception: m was confused with copy or with a numeric count

families.front: What does :bwipeout! remove?
families.back: It removes the current buffer and its window, even when unsaved changes would normally block the action. The exclamation mark forces it.
families.anchor: wipeout is stronger than quit: the buffer itself leaves Vim.
families.shape: :bwipeout! = remove this buffer and window, forcefully

items.prompt: You are in a scratch window with unsaved text. What does :bwipeout! do?
choices: removes the buffer and its window despite unsaved text
saves the buffer under a new name
leaves the buffer and turns off diff mode
why: The force flag allows the buffer and its window to be removed without saving.
Saving needs :w and a path; wipeout does not create a name.
Leaving diff mode is :diffoff!, a different command.
Window removal is a structural action, not a cursor display change.
items.misconception: closing a window was mistaken for safely saving its contents

families.front: What does the ! add to :diffoff!?
families.back: It leaves diff mode in every window, rather than only the current one.
families.anchor: The bang widens the cleanup from this view to all views.
families.shape: :diffoff! = stop diff mode in every window

items.prompt: Two split windows are in diff mode. You run :diffoff!. What is true afterward?
choices: only the active window leaves diff mode
the windows are joined into one
why: The bang form applies the diff-mode exit to every window.
Without the bang, :diffoff affects only the current window.
Deleting buffers is the job of :bwipeout!.
Diff state is cleared without changing the split layout.
items.misconception: the force mark was read as deleting or as having no scope

families.front: Why run :diffthis in each split?
families.back: :diffthis marks the current window as a participant in a side-by-side comparison, so differing cells can be highlighted.
families.anchor: diffthis enrolls this view; it does not edit the text.
families.shape: :diffthis = include the current window in the comparison

items.prompt: After opening two views of related art, what does :diffthis change?
choices: the comparison state of the current view
every differing glyph in the buffer
why: The command enters the current view into Vim's diff comparison; it does not rewrite either buffer.
Highlighting exposes differences but does not replace the glyphs.
Column display is controlled by :set cursorcolumn or :set colorcolumn.
A write command is needed to change the saved file.
items.misconception: visual comparison was confused with an editing command

families.front: What does :g/o/normal! 0rO run?
families.back: It finds every line containing o and runs 0rO in Normal mode on each matching line. The colon command supplies the loop.
families.anchor: g gathers matching rows; normal supplies the small action.
families.shape: :g/pattern/normal! {keys} = run keys on every matching line

items.prompt: Which rows receive 0rO in :g/o/normal! 0rO?
choices: every row whose text contains o
every row that does not contain o
the row at file line o
why: The pattern after g selects matching rows, and normal! applies the keys to each one.
A current-line substitute would use :s without the g command-line loop.
Nonmatching rows are selected with :v, not :g.
The pattern is text to find, not a line number.
items.misconception: :g was read as one search instead of a repeated command

families.front: What does the % after :read stand for?
families.back: Here % names the current file. :read % inserts another copy of that saved file below the cursor.
families.anchor: After :read, percent means this file's name; before s, it means every line.
families.shape: :read % = insert this file below the cursor

items.prompt: In :read %, what is inserted?
choices: a second copy of the current file
every line is selected for substitution
why: The file placeholder after :read expands to the current file path and reads it below the cursor.
Percent before a command is a range, but here it is an argument to read.
The alternate file is #, not %.
A literal percent would be escaped or typed as ordinary text in the buffer.
items.misconception: the same symbol role was carried from a substitute range

families.front: Why set scrollbind in both diff views?
families.back: It makes the bound windows scroll together, keeping corresponding frame rows in view while you inspect differences.
families.anchor: scrollbind ties the viewports, not the text.
families.shape: :set scrollbind = scroll this view with its bound partner

items.prompt: Two side-by-side views are bound. You scroll one downward. What should scrollbind do?
choices: move the partner view by the same amount
rewrite matching rows in the partner buffer
why: scrollbind synchronizes viewport movement so corresponding rows remain aligned.
The option does not copy or edit buffer text.
A ruler is :set colorcolumn, not scrollbind.
Closing a view is a window command or :q, not a display binding.
items.misconception: view synchronization was mistaken for buffer synchronization

families.front: What does :set shiftwidth=1 control?
families.back: It chooses the number of columns moved by indentation commands such as >> and <<.
families.anchor: shiftwidth is the ruler for a shift, not a cursor jump.
families.shape: :set shiftwidth={N} = make >> or << move N columns

items.prompt: With :set shiftwidth=1, what does >> do on the current line?
choices: moves the cursor two columns right
joins it to the next line
why: The shift operator moves the row right by the configured width, here one column.
Cursor motion uses l or a count, not the shift operator.
Deletion is d or x; >> adds indentation.
Joining rows is J, independent of shiftwidth.
items.misconception: the setting was treated as a general movement amount

families.front: What does :silent change about the command that follows?
families.back: :silent suppresses normal messages from the nested command. It does not skip that command or make its edit safe.
families.anchor: silent hides the report, not the work.
families.shape: :silent {command} = run it without messages

items.prompt: What happens when :silent echo 'ready' is run?
choices: the command runs without its usual message
the word ready is inserted at the cursor
why: silent changes message display while still executing the nested command.
The nested command is not cancelled; it still runs.
Buffer removal requires :bwipeout!.
echo reports text; it does not insert buffer text.
items.misconception: silencing output was confused with suppressing execution

families.front: What does :vnew open?
families.back: :vnew creates an empty vertical split, giving you a scratch buffer beside the current view.
families.anchor: vnew means a new vertical neighbor, not a new line in the buffer.
families.shape: :vnew = open an empty window beside this one

items.prompt: After :vnew, what has been created?
choices: an empty window beside the current one
a new line below the cursor
a copy of the current file in the same window
why: The vertical-new command adds a blank neighboring window for scratch work.
Opening a buffer line uses o or O, not :vnew.
Reading a copy uses :read %, while :vnew starts empty.
Comparison begins with :diffthis in windows.
items.misconception: vertical split creation was read as buffer editing

families.front: What does ; repeat after f or t?
families.back: ; repeats the last find in the same direction, using the same target character and find style.
families.anchor: semicolon follows the arrow left by f or t.
families.shape: ; = repeat the last f/t find forward

items.prompt: On a-b-c-d, f- lands on the first dash. What does ; do?
choices: lands on the next dash to the right
searches the whole file for a dash
why: Semicolon repeats the most recent find forward along this row.
Backward repetition is comma.
Whole-file search starts with /, not a find repeat.
Normal-mode ; is a command, not Insert-mode text.
items.misconception: the repeat direction was guessed from punctuation shape

families.front: What does Ctrl-a do on a number?
families.back: Ctrl-a increments the number under or after the cursor by one.
families.anchor: a adds one; Ctrl-x subtracts one.
families.shape: <C-a> = add 1 to the nearby number

items.prompt: The cursor is on the 7 in frame 7. What does Ctrl-a make it?
why: Ctrl-a adds one to the number at the cursor, changing 7 to 8.
Subtracting one is Ctrl-x.
The command edits the number rather than inserting the letter a.
Deletion uses x or d, not Ctrl-a.
items.misconception: Ctrl-a was remembered as text insertion instead of numeric increment

families.front: What kind of Visual area does Ctrl-v start?
families.back: Ctrl-v starts blockwise Visual mode, selecting a rectangle of screen columns across rows.
families.anchor: Ctrl-v cuts a column-shaped window through the art.
families.shape: <C-v> + motion = rectangular Visual block

items.prompt: What does Ctrl-v followed by 2j select?
choices: a rectangular block across three rows
why: Ctrl-v chooses blockwise Visual mode, and 2j extends the rectangle down two rows.
Whole-line Visual mode is V.
Characterwise mode starts with lowercase v.
Window movement uses Ctrl-w commands.
items.misconception: the three Visual modes were treated as interchangeable

families.front: What does Ctrl-w p do with two windows?
families.back: Ctrl-w p moves to the previously active window. The p is an operand to Ctrl-w, not a paste command here.
families.anchor: Ctrl-w hands the next key to the window manager.
families.shape: <C-w>{x} = a window command chosen by {x}

items.prompt: Two splits are open and you just came from the left one. What does Ctrl-w p do?
choices: returns to the previously active split
why: After Ctrl-w, p means the previous window, so focus returns to the left split.
Plain p pastes; Ctrl-w changes the command grammar before p is read.
Paragraph insertion is not a Normal-mode p action.
Line movement uses j or k.
items.misconception: the second key was read without the Ctrl-w prefix

families.front: What does >> do?
families.back: >> shifts the current line right by the configured shiftwidth. << moves it left.
families.anchor: Two greater-than signs push the row toward the right.
families.shape: >> = shift this line right · << = shift left

items.prompt: A row begins in column 1. What visible change does >> make?
choices: moves the cursor to the end of the row
compares the row with its neighbor
why: The doubled greater-than operator shifts the whole row right by shiftwidth.
Deleting a row is dd.
The end-of-row motion is $.
Comparison uses diff commands, not the shift operator.
items.misconception: greater-than was read as a comparison rather than indentation

families.front: What does @q do after a macro was recorded in q?
families.back: @q replays the Normal-mode keys stored in register q once.
families.anchor: At-sign calls the little script; the following letter names it.
families.shape: @{reg} = replay macro {reg} once

items.prompt: Register q contains r= j. What does @q perform?
why: At-sign replays the keys saved in q, so the replacement and downward motion happen in order.
Pasting a register uses "qp.
Recording starts with qq, while @ invokes an existing recording.
A register letter after @ is a name, not a line number.
items.misconception: macro replay was confused with recording or register paste

families.front: How does B move?
families.back: B moves backward to the beginning of the previous space-separated WORD, treating punctuation clusters as part of a WORD.
families.anchor: Capital B walks back by broad WORDs; lowercase b uses ordinary words.
families.shape: B = previous space-separated WORD

items.prompt: On `aa.. bb cc`, the cursor is on c in cc. Where does B land?
choices: the start of the next row
why: B moves to the start of the previous space-separated WORD, bb.
Lowercase b uses a different word grammar around punctuation.
B lands at a WORD start, not its end.
WORD motions stay in the current row unless the file has no more text.
items.misconception: capital WORD motion was read as ordinary lowercase word motion

families.front: What does C do before the typed replacement?
families.back: C deletes from the cursor through the end of the row, enters Insert mode for replacement text, and returns to Normal mode at Esc.
families.anchor: C is a change operator aimed at the row's tail.
families.shape: C{text}<Esc> = replace from cursor to row end

items.prompt: On `abc---` with the cursor on the first dash, what does Cxyz<Esc> leave?
why: C replaces the cursor-to-end tail, so the three dashes become xyz.
Appending after the old tail would require A, not C.
Moving text to the front is not the C command's job.
Esc finishes the replacement; it does not cancel it.
items.misconception: change-to-end was mistaken for append or whole-row replacement

families.front: What does D delete?
families.back: D deletes from the cursor to the end of the current row, leaving the prefix before the cursor intact.
families.anchor: D drives the row's tail away.
families.shape: D = delete cursor through row end

items.prompt: The row is `abc---` and the cursor is on the first dash. What remains after D?
why: D removes the cursor and everything to its right, leaving abc.
D does not keep the deleted tail.
Only deleting from column 1 would clear the whole row.
The command makes a visible deletion, so the original row does not remain.
items.misconception: the direction or retained side of D was reversed

families.front: Where does E stop?
families.back: E moves to the end of the next space-separated WORD, using the broad WORD grammar of capital motions.
families.anchor: E = end of a broad WORD; W and B use the same capital grammar.
families.shape: E = end of the next space-separated WORD

items.prompt: On `aa.. bb`, with the cursor on the first a, where does E land?
choices: the end of the current row
why: Capital E travels to the final character of the next space-separated WORD, bb.
The start of bb is W's destination, not E's.
Punctuation remains in the first WORD cluster here.
E stops at the next WORD end, which is before the row end.
items.misconception: WORD start and WORD end destinations were swapped

families.front: What does Ctrl-r do inside Replace mode?
families.back: In Replace mode, Ctrl-r followed by a register letter inserts that register's contents at the current replacement position.
families.anchor: The same Ctrl-r glyph has a different job in Replace mode: paste a register.
families.shape: R<C-r>{reg}<Esc> = replace while pasting register {reg}

items.prompt: Register a contains `*`. What does R Ctrl-r a Esc place at the replacement point?
why: Replace-mode Ctrl-r asks for a register and types its stored text.
Ctrl-r is interpreted by Vim as a register insertion in this mode.
Undo history is reached with u, g- or :earlier.
The register contents, not just its name, are inserted.
items.misconception: Ctrl-r's Normal-mode redo meaning was carried into Replace mode

families.front: Where does T- stop?
families.back: T- searches backward along the current row and stops just after the previous dash, one cell on the cursor side.
families.anchor: Lowercase t stops before a target going right; capital T stops after a target going left.
families.shape: T{char} = backward find, stop just after {char}

items.prompt: On `a-b-c`, the cursor is on c. Where does T- land?
choices: on b, just after the dash
at the end of the row
why: Capital T walks left to the dash and stops on the cell immediately after it, b.
F- lands on the target itself; T's stop is offset from it.
The earlier dash is not the nearest target from c.
The motion stays near the found dash rather than jumping to row end.
items.misconception: the target cell and the just-after stopping cell were conflated

families.front: What does uppercase V select?
families.back: V starts linewise Visual mode. Extending the selection adds whole rows, not a rectangle of individual cells.
families.anchor: Capital V selects whole rows from edge to edge.
families.shape: V + motion = whole-line selection

items.prompt: What does V2j select?
choices: a rectangular block three columns wide
why: V makes the selection linewise, and 2j extends it through two more rows.
Characterwise selection starts with lowercase v.
Blockwise selection starts with Ctrl-v.
Window movement uses Ctrl-w.
items.misconception: uppercase and lowercase Visual modes were swapped

families.front: What does A do to a Visual block?
families.back: In a Visual block, A appends the typed text at the right edge of every selected row, then Esc applies it.
families.anchor: Visual A repeats an append across the selected rows.
families.shape: Visual A{text}<Esc> = append text to every selected row

items.prompt: A block covers three rows. After $A|<Esc>, where is the bar on each row?
choices: at the end of every selected row
at the start of every selected row
inside the existing text at the cursor
why: Visual A appends the typed bar to the right edge of each row in the block.
Adding at the left edge uses Visual I.
The block operation repeats over all selected rows, not just the anchor row.
A moves to the row end before typing rather than inserting at the old cursor cell.
items.misconception: Visual append was read as a one-row or left-edge insert

families.front: What does I do to a Visual block?
families.back: In a Visual block, I inserts the typed text before the block on every selected row, then Esc applies the same insertion across the rows.
families.anchor: Visual I builds a left edge across the selection.
families.shape: Visual I{text}<Esc> = insert text before each selected row block

items.prompt: A three-row column is selected. What does Visual I|<Esc> do?
choices: adds | before the selected column on all three rows
why: Visual I repeats the insertion at the selection's left edge for every row.
Appending after rows is Visual A.
A block selection carries the operation through all selected rows.
Deletion would use x or d while the selection is active.
items.misconception: the two blockwise insertion edges were reversed

families.front: What does Visual c change?
families.back: Visual c replaces the selected cells on every selected row with the typed text, and Esc finishes the block edit.
families.anchor: c clears the rectangle before filling it with the replacement.
families.shape: Visual c{text}<Esc> = replace each selected block

items.prompt: A one-column block spans three rows. What does Visual c=<Esc> leave?
choices: = in that column on all three rows
the old cells plus = after them
the entire three rows replaced by one =
why: Visual c applies the replacement to every cell in the selected column across the rows.
The selected block, not just its first cell, receives the edit.
Change replaces the cells instead of appending after them.
Line structure stays intact; a block edit does not collapse rows.
items.misconception: Visual change was reduced to a single-cell or append action

families.front: What does r= do on a Visual selection?
families.back: Visual r replaces every selected character with the one character you type, preserving the selection's shape.
families.anchor: Visual r paints the chosen glyph across the selection.
families.shape: Visual r{char} = replace every selected cell with {char}

items.prompt: Three characters are selected. What does r= do?
choices: turns all three selected cells into =
replaces only the cell under the cursor
starts Replace mode for the whole file
why: Visual r applies one replacement glyph to every selected character.
Normal r changes one cell; the Visual selection broadens its reach.
Replacement preserves the selected width rather than inserting cells.
The command is scoped to the current selection, not the file.
items.misconception: Normal r's one-cell scope was carried into Visual mode

families.front: What does y do after Visual selection?
families.back: Visual y copies the selected characters, rows or block into the unnamed register without changing the buffer.
families.anchor: Selection first, y copies exactly the selected shape.
families.shape: Visual y = yank the current selection

items.prompt: After V2j, what does y copy?
choices: the next three rows without their line breaks
why: Linewise Visual mode defines the selection, and y copies that selection.
A single character copy would be yl or a characterwise selection.
The selection is local; y does not silently expand to the file.
Linewise yanking preserves row boundaries.
items.misconception: the operator's scope was detached from the active Visual selection

families.front: How does W differ from w?
families.back: W moves to the beginning of the next space-separated WORD, so punctuation stays inside a WORD instead of splitting it.
families.anchor: Capital W sees spaces; lowercase w sees word punctuation.
families.shape: W = next space-separated WORD

items.prompt: On `aa.. bb`, starting at the first a, where does W land?
why: W skips to the next space-separated WORD, which starts at b.
Punctuation within aa.. remains in the same broad WORD.
The end of bb is E's destination.
W finds a WORD start before the row's final cell.
items.misconception: capital W was assumed to split punctuation like lowercase w

families.front: What does 2 Ctrl-a do?
families.back: A count repeats the increment twice, so the nearby number increases by two.
families.anchor: The count sits before Ctrl-a and multiplies its one-step change.
families.shape: [count]<C-a> = add count to the nearby number

items.prompt: The cursor is on 7. What does 2 Ctrl-a make it?
why: Each Ctrl-a adds one and the leading 2 repeats it twice, making 7 become 9.
One increment would be Ctrl-a without the count.
The count is repetition, not digit concatenation.
The command performs two changes, so the number does not stay put.
items.misconception: the count was treated as a prefix digit instead of repetition

families.front: What does 3@q do?
families.back: It replays macro q three times in succession.
families.anchor: The number before @ counts replays, not keys inside the macro.
families.shape: [count]@{reg} = replay macro {reg} count times

items.prompt: Macro q contains r= j. What sequence does 3@q run?
choices: r= j, r= j, r= j
r= three times, then j once
why: The count repeats the complete stored macro, including both its replacement and motion.
A count before an individual key would be written inside the macro itself.
Recording uses q at the start, not @.
Pasting a register needs the quote prefix and p.
items.misconception: the count was applied to only the first key of the macro

families.front: Where does 2B go?
families.back: 2B moves backward across two broad space-separated WORD starts.
families.anchor: The count repeats B's whole WORD-sized jump.
families.shape: [count]B = move back count WORDs

items.prompt: On `aa bb cc dd`, the cursor starts on dd. Where does 2B land?
why: The first B reaches cc and the second reaches the start of bb.
One backward WORD jump from dd reaches cc; two are needed to reach bb.
The motion crosses WORD starts rather than staying on the original WORD.
Column 1 is 0, not the result of a counted B here.
items.misconception: a counted backward WORD motion was pictured as a line jump

families.front: What does 2W count?
families.back: 2W advances to the beginning of the second next space-separated WORD.
families.anchor: W hops WORD starts; the count says how many hops.
families.shape: [count]W = move forward count WORDs

items.prompt: On `aa bb cc dd`, starting at aa, where does 2W land?
why: W reaches bb on its first hop and cc on its second.
bb is one WORD away, so it would be 1W.
dd is the third next WORD from aa.
W moves forward to another WORD start, not backward within aa.
items.misconception: the count was mistaken for a line or character count

families.front: What does 2dd delete?
families.back: 2dd deletes the current line and the next line as one counted whole-line operation.
families.anchor: The number before doubled d counts rows, not characters.
families.shape: [count]dd = delete count whole lines

items.prompt: On rows A, B, C with the cursor on B, what remains after 2dd?
choices: row B with its text shortened
why: The count removes B and the following whole row C, leaving A.
The two deleted rows are consecutive, not separated by A.
C is part of the deletion because dd is linewise.
Character deletion would use x; doubled d removes whole rows.
items.misconception: the count was read as columns or as a nonconsecutive selection

families.front: What does ci( change?
families.back: ci( deletes the text inside the nearest parentheses and enters Insert mode for the replacement, leaving the parentheses themselves.
families.anchor: c changes; i keeps the inside; the object supplies the pair.
families.shape: ci{object} = change inside the object

items.prompt: On `(old)`, with the cursor inside, what does ci(new<Esc> leave?
why: The inside text is replaced while the surrounding parentheses stay in place.
ci( does not prepend outside the pair.
The old inside text is deleted before new is typed.
Around-the-object change would remove the pair too; inside keeps it.
items.misconception: inside and around object scope were mixed up

families.front: What does da( remove?
families.back: da( deletes the text and the surrounding parentheses of the nearest pair.
families.anchor: d deletes; a means around, so the fence comes out too.
families.shape: da{object} = delete around the object

items.prompt: On `x(old)y`, with the cursor on o, what remains after da(?
why: Around-the-pair deletion removes old and both parentheses, leaving x and y.
The empty pair would remain if only the inside were deleted.
The text is part of the deleted object.
da( does not extract the inside; it removes it.
items.misconception: around was interpreted as inside-only deletion

families.front: What does dd remove?
families.back: dd deletes the entire current line and places the cursor on a nearby remaining line.
families.anchor: Doubled d is linewise: one d starts delete, the second names a whole line.
families.shape: dd = delete this whole line

items.prompt: Rows A, B, C have the cursor on B. What remains after dd?
choices: the characters after the cursor on B
why: dd removes row B as a whole, leaving the other rows adjacent.
The current row is the one deleted, not retained alone.
Doubled d is an editing command, so the rows do change.
Deleting a row tail uses D; dd is linewise.
items.misconception: linewise deletion was confused with tail deletion

families.front: How does gR differ from R?
families.back: gR overwrites screen cells in Virtual Replace mode, preserving the width of wide glyphs and tabs more carefully than ordinary R.
families.anchor: The g prefix makes replacement respect screen cells.
families.shape: gR{text}<Esc> = overwrite screen cells, then Esc

items.prompt: What is the purpose of gR==<Esc> on rows containing a wide glyph?
choices: overwrite screen cells without pulling later cells left
insert two new characters before the glyph
why: Virtual Replace treats the visible cells as the layout to preserve while overwriting.
Insertion would shift later text, which replacement avoids.
The command remains local to the current replacement run.
Undo is u, not gR.
items.misconception: virtual replacement was treated as insertion or ordinary undo

families.front: Where does g_ stop?
families.back: g_ moves to the last non-blank character on the row, while $ can land on trailing spaces after it.
families.anchor: The underscore hugs the last visible glyph; dollar reaches the row's physical end.
families.shape: g_ = last nonblank cell · $ = final cell

items.prompt: On `ab   `, where do g_ and $ land?
choices: g_ on b; $ on the last space
g_ on the first space; $ on b
why: g_ ignores trailing blanks and $ uses the physical row end.
Dollar does not skip the visible trailing spaces.
The last nonblank is b, not a space before it.
Neither command is the column-one motion 0.
items.misconception: row end and last visible glyph were treated as the same cell

families.front: What does ga report?
families.back: ga displays information about the character under the cursor, including its character and numeric representations, without changing the buffer.
families.anchor: a asks what the glyph is; it does not alter it.
families.shape: ga = inspect the character under the cursor

items.prompt: What happens when ga is pressed on a middle dot?
choices: Vim reports the glyph and its numeric value
the dot is replaced by a
the cursor jumps to the next dot
why: ga is an inspection command that prints character information and leaves the cell intact.
Replacing one cell uses r followed by a glyph.
Deletion uses x or d.
Searching for another dot needs f. or a pattern search.
items.misconception: the inspection key was mistaken for an edit

families.front: What does gv restore?
families.back: gv reselects the exact area from the previous Visual operation, using the same character, line or block mode.
families.anchor: g remembers the last Visual shape; v brings that shape back.
families.shape: gv = reselect the previous Visual area

items.prompt: You just changed a rectangular block and moved away. What does gv do?
why: gv restores the previous Visual boundaries and mode so the selection can be used again.
A new selection begins with v, V or Ctrl-v.
Repeating the edit is dot; gv only selects.
The last line is G.
items.misconception: Visual history was confused with edit repetition or file motion

families.front: What does n do after a search?
families.back: n moves to the next match in the direction of the last search. N moves to the previous match.
families.anchor: n means next in the search trail.
families.shape: n = next match · N = previous match

items.prompt: After /o<CR> lands on the first o, what does n do?
choices: moves to the next o in the search direction
starts a new search for n
why: n reuses the active search and advances to its next match.
A new search would begin with /.
N reverses the direction to the previous match.
In Normal mode n is a search command, not inserted text.
items.misconception: n was read as a literal key instead of search continuation

families.front: What does i do before the typed text?
families.back: i enters Insert mode before the cursor. The following text is inserted there until Esc returns to Normal mode.
families.anchor: i inserts in front; Esc closes the typing interval.
families.shape: i{text}<Esc> = insert text before the cursor

items.prompt: On `ac` with the cursor on c, what does i b Esc make?
why: i places the typed b before the cursor's c, producing abc.
Appending after c uses a, not i.
The original a remains before the inserted b.
Esc ends Insert mode after the change has been made.
items.misconception: insert-before and append-after were swapped

families.front: What does lowercase w count as a word?
families.back: w moves to the start of the next ordinary word, with punctuation and word characters able to form separate runs.
families.anchor: Lowercase w notices punctuation; W treats spaces as the boundary.
families.shape: w = next ordinary word start

items.prompt: On `aa.. bb`, where can lowercase w stop before W reaches bb?
choices: at a punctuation run such as the dots
at the end of the row
why: Lowercase w can treat punctuation as its own word run, so the dots are a possible next start.
Capital W skips directly across the space-separated WORD.
w seeks a next word start before the row necessarily ends.
The command is a row motion here, not a line jump.
items.misconception: lowercase word grammar was assumed to match capital WORD grammar

families.front: How do qq ... q and @q work together?
families.back: The first q plus a register starts recording Normal keys, the final q stops, and @q later replays what was captured.
families.anchor: q writes a tiny script; @ calls it back.
families.shape: q{reg}...q = record into a register · @{reg} = replay

items.prompt: What is stored by qqr=jq?
choices: r= followed by j in register q
the current row in register r
why: The opening qq selects register q for recording, the middle keys are captured, and the closing q stops.
The q presses mark recording boundaries rather than becoming the macro body.
Register r is not selected by this command.
Search begins with /, so = is simply a recorded key here.
items.misconception: recording boundaries were mistaken for the macro's body

families.front: What does r Ctrl-k .M type?
families.back: It replaces the character under the cursor with the digraph glyph .M, a middle dot, without requiring that glyph on the keyboard.
families.anchor: Ctrl-k joins two mnemonic letters into one glyph.
families.shape: r<C-k>{a}{b} = replace one cell with a digraph

items.prompt: On `(o)`, what does r Ctrl-k .M do at o?
choices: types the four visible keys into the row
moves to the middle of the window
why: The digraph .M resolves to a middle-dot glyph and r replaces one cell with it.
Ctrl-k is a composition instruction, not literal buffer text here.
The M is part of the digraph, not the window-middle motion.
Dot repeat is a separate lone Normal-mode command.
items.misconception: the digraph keystrokes were split into unrelated Normal commands

families.front: Where does t- stop?
families.back: t- searches forward along the current row and stops just before the next dash.
families.anchor: t takes you to the doorstep of the target; f lands on it.
families.shape: t{char} = forward find, stop just before {char}

items.prompt: On `a-b`, the cursor is on a. Where does t- land?
choices: on a, just before the dash
why: The target dash is next, and t stops on the cell immediately before it, a.
f- lands on the dash itself.
Moving beyond the target would require another motion.
t is a find motion near the target, not a jump to $.
items.misconception: t's offset stop was confused with f's target stop

families.front: What does lowercase v start?
families.back: v starts characterwise Visual mode, where the selection grows by individual cells.
families.anchor: Lowercase v selects visible characters; V selects whole rows.
families.shape: v + motion = characterwise selection

items.prompt: What does v2l select from the first cell?
why: Characterwise v starts at one cell and 2l extends through two more cells.
Whole rows require uppercase V.
A rectangle requires Ctrl-v.
Reselecting an old area is gv.
items.misconception: the characterwise and linewise Visual starters were swapped

families.front: What does ya( include?
families.back: ya( copies the text inside the nearest parentheses together with the parentheses themselves.
families.anchor: y copies; a wraps the object in the selection.
families.shape: ya{object} = yank around the object

items.prompt: On `x(old)y`, what text does ya( place in the register?
choices: the character under the cursor only
why: Around-the-object yank includes both the inside and its parentheses.
Inside-only yank would use yi(.
The surrounding x and y are outside the object.
The object spans more than one character here.
items.misconception: around-yank was confused with inside-yank or a line yank

families.front: What does zp preserve when it pastes a block?
families.back: zp pastes a yanked block after the cursor without manufacturing trailing spaces to pad short rows.
families.anchor: z keeps the block's honest edges; p places it after.
families.shape: zp = paste a block after without padding short rows

items.prompt: Why choose zp for rows with different visible widths?
choices: it pastes after the cursor without adding trailing blanks
it pastes before the cursor and pads every row
why: The z paste form keeps short rows short instead of filling their unused width.
Putting before uses zP, while padding is precisely what zp avoids.
Yanking uses y and does not paste anything.
A split is created with :vnew or :vsplit.
items.misconception: the z prefix was treated as an alternate yank or window command

families.front: What does zy change about a block yank?
families.back: zy copies a Visual block without including trailing spaces that merely pad shorter rows.
families.anchor: z trims the invisible tail; y still yanks.
families.shape: zy = yank a Visual block without trailing padding

items.prompt: Rows `ab` and `abcd` are in a two-row block. What does zy avoid copying?
choices: the two padding spaces after ab
why: zy keeps the shorter row's visible content but drops spaces that only fill the wider rectangle.
The actual glyphs remain part of the block.
Both selected rows are copied.
Row structure is retained; only invisible padding is omitted.
items.misconception: tight block yank was mistaken for deleting visible cells

families.front: Where does } move in frame-separated art?
families.back: } moves forward to the next blank-line boundary, taking you to the end of the current frame or toward the next frame.
families.anchor: A brace hops between blank-line-separated frames.
families.shape: } = next frame boundary · { = previous boundary

items.prompt: The cursor is inside the first frame, and a blank row separates it from the next. What does } do?
choices: moves toward the next frame boundary
jumps to the last line of the file
why: } is the forward paragraph/frame motion and uses the blank row as its boundary.
The file-bottom motion is G, while } follows a blank-row boundary.
A single-row move is j; } can cross several rows.
The brace is a Normal-mode motion, not text deletion.
items.misconception: frame motion was reduced to a one-row move or a file jump

families.front: What does :vsplit show beside the current view?
families.back: With no file name, :vsplit opens another view of the same buffer. Both windows show the same text, so an edit appears in both.
families.anchor: split the view, not the art.
families.shape: :vsplit = two neighboring views of the same text

items.prompt: You run :vsplit without a file name. What is in the new window?
choices: another view of the same buffer
an extra row below the cursor
a separate saved copy of the art
why: Both windows display the same buffer, with independent cursor positions.
An empty neighboring buffer is opened with :vnew.
A new text row is opened with o, not a window split.
Splitting does not create or save a separate file.
items.misconception: a new view was mistaken for new text

families.front: What does :q close when two windows show the same saved art?
families.back: :q closes the current window. The other window remains open with the same buffer; the command does not erase the art.
families.anchor: quit this view; keep the neighboring view.
families.shape: :q = close the current window

items.prompt: Two windows show the same saved art. You run :q in one. What remains?
choices: the other window still shows the art
the art is deleted from disk
why: With another window open, :q closes only the current view.
Quitting all windows uses :qa, not :q.
Closing a window does not delete a saved file.
Deleting a row uses dd, not :q.
items.misconception: closing a window was confused with deleting its text

families.front: What does # mean after :read?
families.back: Here # names the alternate file: usually the file you visited before this one. :read # inserts its saved text below the cursor, without opening a new window.
families.anchor: percent is this file; hash is the alternate file.
families.shape: :read # = insert the alternate file below the cursor

items.prompt: A reference file is the alternate file. What does :read # insert?
choices: the saved reference text below the cursor
another copy of the current file
why: Hash expands to the alternate file name, and read inserts that file's text below this row.
The current file placeholder is %, not #.
Hash is a file placeholder here, not inserted text.
Reading text changes this buffer; :vnew opens an empty window.
items.misconception: the alternate file placeholder was confused with the current file
